description: Birds in data/uk_birds_top200.json with no plate in the plate database, generated by scripts/missing_plates.py -- run it again after every build rather than editing this file. Rank is how often the species is reported here, so the gaps cost different amounts: when a bird with no plate is the headline, the board falls back to a Wikimedia photograph, and a bird at rank 6 leads the board far more often than one at rank 98. `searched_no_plate` means the builder looked and found nothing usable in the corpus it currently searches, which is a corpus that can be widened; `excluded` means a plate was found, looked at and refused, with the reason carried through from data/plate_exclusions.json; `not_yet_searched` are ranks the builder has not reached, which is not the same as missing.

refused.file: Coloured figures of the birds of the British Islands - issued by Lord Lilford (Plate XXIII) (20132195059).jpg
refused.reason: The gull is preening, head buried in its wing, so the one thing that says gull -- the bill and the eye -- is upside down inside the feathers. Pale grey bird on pale sand, three more birds behind it, and a wide scene at that: at 480px it is a grey shape on a yellow beach.

refused.work: Coloured figures of the birds of the British Islands
refused.reason: Lilford's herring gull is the preening bird with its head inside its wing, and Commons holds scan after scan of that one plate, so excluding a file just hands over the next copy. Nothing else in Lilford shows the bird, and a headless grey shape on a yellow beach is not worth a plate.

Keulemans drew the black-headed gull for this journal three times and every one is the same gullery seen across a lake: a hundred birds forty pixels wide. Correctly identified and genuinely his, and unreadable as a portrait on a 480px panel. No plate is better than a grey landscape.

A landscape with a swan in it. Reeds, a far bank, a wide band of water, and the swan white on the white of the water with only its bill to say which end is the front. The board wants a bird; this is a view.

What replaced the swan-in-a-landscape, and worse: the swan swims white against white water, the cutout finds no edge between them and walks up the neck, and the board gets a white shape with no head on it and the reeds still attached.

refused.work: Coloured figures of the birds of the British Islands
refused.reason: Lilford's swan swims with two cygnets, and white on white water is the one thing this panel cannot print: the whole bird arrives as a single pale oval with an orange bill floating in the middle of it and no line anywhere to say where the swan stops and the lake starts. Onze vogels had already failed the same way, with the cutout taking the head off. Refused as a work because Commons holds several scans of the one Lilford plate.
A study of a tawny owl's talons -- four claws on a blank page. Right artist, right bird, and nothing in the filename to say so.

refused.file: Poecile montanus songarus & Poecile montanus affinis & Poecile superciliosus 1889.jpg
refused.reason: The third of the 1889 pages, and the same shape: five birds, three named taxa, two of them races of willow tit from central Asia and the third a white-browed tit. A page from a monograph, not a portrait.

refused.work: Nauchnye rezulʹtaty puteshestvyǐ N.M. Przhevalʹskago po t͡sentralʹnoǐ Azii
refused.reason: And the same again: songarus, the Songar tit, rusty-flanked and drawn with the next bird on the plate clipped in under its feet.

refused.file: Coloured figures of the birds of the British Islands - issued by Lord Lilford (20728475732).jpg
refused.reason: A white bird in front of dead reeds. On paper the egret is a beautiful cloud of plumes; at six inks the plumes and the reeds dither into the same speckle and the bird disappears into the bed it is standing in.

refused.file: Coloured figures of the birds of the British Islands - issued by Lord Lilford (Plate XXV) (20130813418).jpg
refused.reason: A fine plate that the cutout beheads. The gull is standing with its white head and neck against the pale shore, the head is the same tone as the paper and joined to it, so the flood fill walks straight up the neck and takes the lot: what lands on the board is a black-backed body on pink legs with nothing above the shoulders.

refused.work: Coloured figures of the birds of the British Islands
refused.reason: Lilford drew this gull once and Commons holds half a dozen scans of that one plate, so excluding a file only moves the builder onto the next copy of the same picture. The bird stands with its white head against pale sand, the head is paper-coloured and joined to the paper, and the cutout takes it away every time. The plate is not at fault; we simply cannot use it, and a headless gull is worse than a photograph.

refused.file: Coloured figures of the birds of the British Islands - issued by Lord Lilford (Plate XXII) (20310404102).jpg
refused.reason: The same beheading as the great black-backed gull, on the same shore-and-sand background, and here it takes the bill as well. What is left is a grey mantle on one leg in a lot of empty sand -- more beach than bird even before the head went.

refused.work: Coloured figures of the birds of the British Islands
refused.reason: The same plate, the same white head on the same pale shore, the same beheading in every scan of it. Refused as a work for the same reason as the great black-backed gull: there is nothing else in Lilford for this bird to fall back to.

refused.file: Coloured figures of the birds of the British Islands - issued by Lord Lilford (Plate XXIX) (20318870755).jpg
refused.reason: Two whole kittiwakes on a nest, and beside them a tall pale stripe the scanner caught at the edge of the facing page. It survives the cutout as its own blob, so the board would carry a vertical rule standing to the right of the birds like a doorframe.

A floating cask in a heavy sea with a dozen kittiwakes on and around it, sky to the top of the page. The same failure this journal gives the black-headed gull -- a seascape with birds in it rather than a bird -- and at 480px the cask reads better than any of them.

Keulemans, from Godman's monograph of the petrels, and it is a white-faced storm petrel: white below, a dark mask through the eye, long legs and yellow-webbed feet. Ours is sooty all over with a white rump. The file is named after the volume rather than the bird, so nothing but the picture gives it away.

The second wrong petrel in a row, and a closer one: a Guadalupe storm petrel, forked-tailed and all dark where ours carries a white rump, from an island in the Pacific and extinct since about 1912. Every Keulemans petrel on Commons is a portrait of some petrel, and the search cannot tell which.

This one does contain our bird -- and a Wilson's petrel beside it, and a downy chick, and the German caption naming all three, and a ruled white border the cutout cannot get past, so the whole page arrives as a rectangle. Two species and a block of type is a page from a book, not a portrait.

Mother Carey herself: a witch on a broomstick over a wrecking sea, with a hundred petrels the size of commas around her and rays of light coming through the cloud. A famous plate and a lovely one, and the bird in it is a motif rather than a subject. After two wrong petrel species this was the third refusal for this bird, and it is the point at which no plate is the right answer.

Not a scan of a plate but a photograph of an open book: page edges, binding, the shadow of the gutter. The cutout has no paper to remove and keeps the whole spread, captions and all -- and the captions are two species, the Chatham Island snipe next to the godwit.

Three curlews on a rock, and the one in the middle -- the one the plate is named for and drawn around -- is a slender-billed curlew. The whimbrels are the supporting cast. A painted sky and sea behind them as well, so there is nothing to cut away either.
